OPINION
Representing the Parties:
For Appellant: T. Ryan
For Respondent: Rachel Glass, Attorney
For Office of Tax Appeals: Andrew Jacobson, Attorney
N. RALSTON, Administrative Law Judge: Pursuant to Revenue and Taxation Code
(R&TC) section 19324, T. Ryan (appellant) appeals an action by the Franchise Tax Board
(respondent) denying appellant’s claim for refund of $2,239 for the 2020 tax year.
Appellant waived the right to an oral hearing; therefore, this matter was submitted to the
Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) on the written record pursuant to California Code of Regulations,
title 18, section 30209(a).
ISSUE
Whether appellant’s refund claim for the 2020 tax year is barred by the statute of
limitations.
FACTUAL FINDINGS
1. On August 15, 2025, appellant late-filed a 2020 California Resident Income Tax Return
(2020 Return), claiming withholdings of $2,622 and requesting a refund of $2,239.
2. Respondent treated the 2020 Return as a claim for refund, which respondent denied
because it was filed after the statute of limitations had expired.
3. Subsequently, appellant filed this appeal.

DISCUSSION
California law generally requires that taxpayers file their refund claims by the later of:
(1) four years from the date the return is filed, if filed within the extended filing period pursuant to
an extension; (2) four years from the due date of the return without regard to any extensions; or
(3) one year from the date of overpayment. (R&TC, § 19306(a).) A withholding credit made
before the due date of the return is generally deemed paid on the original due date of the return.
(R&TC, § 19002(c)(1).) Taxpayers have the burden of proof to show entitlement to a refund and
that the claim is timely. (Appeal of Benemi Partners, L.P., 2020-OTA-144P.)
Appellant did not file his 2020 return until August 15, 2025, and therefore his claim for
refund was not timely under any of the above-referenced statute of limitations periods.
Regarding the first four-year statute of limitations period, appellant did not file his 2020 return by
October 15, 2021, the extended due date for his 2020 return. (R&TC, § 18567(a)(1); Cal. Code
Regs., tit. 18, § 18567(a).) Accordingly, the first four-year statute of limitations period is
inapplicable. Regarding the second four-year statute of limitations period, appellant filed his
2020 return claiming a refund of tax on August 15, 2025, more than four years after the original
due date for the return of April 15, 2021. (R&TC, §§ 18566, 19306(a).) Therefore, the claim for
refund was filed outside of the second four-year statute of limitations. As to the one-year statute
of limitations period, appellant’s withholdings of $2,622 are deemed to have been paid on the
original due date of the return (April 15, 2021). (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 18, § 19002(d)(1).)
Appellant’s 2025 Return, which respondent received on August 15, 2025, was not filed within
one year of April 15, 2021. Accordingly, appellant’s claim for refund is also untimely under the
one-year limitations period.
Appellant asserts that the due date for the 2020 tax year was extended to
October 15, 2021, due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Appellant asserts that the deadline for his
claim for refund was October 15, 2025, which means that the 2020 Return filed on
August 15, 2025, was within the first four-year statute of limitations.
Appellant correctly points out that respondent altered the due date of the return by
postponing the filing deadline for 2020 tax return. However, the deadline was postponed to
May 17, 2021, not October 15, 2021. Treasury Regulation section 301.7508A-1(b)(4) provides
that the postponement period will not change the due date of the return. Thus, respondent’s
postponement of the original filing due date to May 17, 2021, did not change the original due
date of April 15, 2021, upon which the four-year statute of limitations for refund claims is based.
(Appeal of Nguyen, 2025-OTA-333P; Appeal of Bannon, 2023-OTA-096P.)

To the extent appellant is arguing that he can file a claim for refund within four years
from the automatic extension due date of October 15, 2021, appellant misunderstands the law.
California allows individuals an automatic six-month extension of the time to file a return, which
sets an extended due date of October 15, 2021, for 2020 tax returns that are filed within the
extension period. (R&TC, § 18567(a)(1); Cal. Code Regs., tit. 18, § 18567(a); see also Appeal
of Bannon, supra.) However, if the return is not filed within six months of the original due date,
no extension is allowed. (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 18, § 18567(a).) As previously noted, appellant’s
2020 Return filed on August 15, 2025, does not meet the requirements for the first four-year
statute of limitations. Thus, appellant’s claim for refund dated August 15, 2025, is untimely.
HOLDING
Appellant’s refund claim for the 2020 tax year is barred by the statute of limitations.
DISPOSITION
Respondent’s action denying appellant’s claim for refund is sustained.
Natasha Ralston
Administrative Law Judge
